name: Belotero Revive

card.summary: A Merz skin-booster injectable of lightly cross-linked hyaluronic acid with glycerol, given in small superficial injections to improve skin hydration, elasticity and glow rather than to add volume.
card.note: Injectable procedure performed by a clinician; bruising, swelling and rare vascular events are documented risks of HA injections.

quick.overview:
Belotero Revive is a hyaluronic-acid skin booster from Merz that combines slightly cross-linked HA (20 mg/ml) with glycerol (17.5 mg/ml). It is injected in tiny amounts into the skin to improve hydration, elasticity and overall skin quality, so skin looks smoother and fresher, instead of reshaping the face as a volumising filler does.

Published work consists of small studies. A split-face study of 24 healthy women compared it with another HA skin booster and reported improvement from baseline in surface hydration, elasticity, water loss and melanin readings for both products. A 2025 retrospective cohort of 40 patients used microcannula delivery and assessed hydration and firmness with corneometry and ultrasound elastography.
quick.how: A clinician places the product in the skin with fine needles or a microcannula, often in a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. The split-face study used three treatment sessions and followed patients to week 14, while the retrospective cohort compared one session with two.
quick.risks: HA injections can cause pain, bruising, redness and swelling, and, more rarely, vascular occlusion or granulomatous reactions. It is a medical procedure and its availability and labelling vary by country.

lead: Belotero Revive is an injectable skin booster developed by Merz. It contains cohesive polydensified matrix hyaluronic acid with glycerol, abbreviated CPM-HA20G, a slightly cross-linked HA at 20 mg/ml with 17.5 mg/ml glycerol [1]. It is used for skin quality, meaning hydration, elasticity and radiance, as distinct from volume restoration [2].

In appearance terms, a skin booster targets the skin surface. People seek it for a smoother, more hydrated look and what clinics call 'glow'. The hyaluronic acid draws water, and the glycerol is added as a humectant [1][3].

Published studies include a split-face comparison with another HA product [1] and a retrospective cohort using microcannula delivery with objective skin measurements [2]. Both are small, and no large randomized trial is cited here.

chain: Small HA-plus-glycerol injections placed in the skin

angle.text: Instead of adding volume under the face, a booster treats the skin itself. Studies measure hydration, elasticity and firmness, which are the properties people associate with fresher-looking skin.

paras: The product is a slightly cross-linked HA gel mixed with glycerol, described as CPM-HA20G [1]. Hyaluronic acid generally absorbs water and swells into a gel; manufacturers cross-link it to slow breakdown, which lengthens duration compared with native HA [3].

Skin boosters are for skin quality improvement, as opposed to filling folds or reshaping contours [1][2]. Reported goals include hydration, elasticity, firmness and reduced transepidermal water loss [1][2].

A 2022 split-face, single-blinded study enrolled 24 healthy women; HCC (Profhilo) was injected on the right cheek and CPM-HA20G (Belotero Revive) on the left in three sessions, with measurements at baseline and weeks 1, 8 and 14. Both products showed effect relative to baseline on surface hydration, elasticity, transepidermal water loss and melanin [1].

A 2025 retrospective cohort of 40 patients compared one or two sessions of microcannula-delivered CPM-R, assessing results at day 30 after the final treatment with corneometry, ultrasound strain elastography, the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale and pain and comfort scales [2].

Possible complications of HA injection in general include nerve and microvessel injury, pain, bruising, redness, itching and vascular occlusion; some fillers cause a granulomatous foreign-body reaction [3].
